meta.operativeContentRazor: This file records THAT a text sets out a procedure — its type, its structural anatomy, how complete it is and on what evidence, its edition/PD situation, and its harm profile. It transcribes NO mantra syllables, NO seed-syllable strings, NO yantra as a usable template, NO ingredient, NO quantity, NO repetition-count, NO timing, NO target-naming formula, and contains NO second-person directive. Sources read for this slice DO print all of those things (Ullrey translates mantras, counts, substances and coercive sanctions in full, by explicit methodological choice at pp. 146 and 152); none of it is carried across. Where a structural feature can only be described by naming a slot — e.g. that hostile mantras carry a placeholder standing for the target's name — the slot is described and the tokens are withheld.
meta.harmFraming: The ṣaṭkarman includes māraṇa (killing) and vaśīkaraṇa (subjugation), and much of this corpus is organised AROUND them: two of the three Uḍḍīśatantra recensions open their body-text with murder, not with pacification. This is catalogued as academic religious history under the repo's abhicāra-wing precedent (see FRAMING; abhichara-data.js FRAMING.label/care). Efficacy is never asserted — the tradition CLAIMS, the text SAYS. Ullrey, the slice's principal source, states flatly at p. 633: 'Magic doesn't work.' Rites in this corpus target NAMED LIVING PERSONS by design; that is recorded as a fact about the texts and is the single largest reason no procedure detail crosses into this file.
meta.livingPeopleNote: Several actors here are living or recent and several disputes are current: the Hindi commentators Śivadatta Miśra (1998) and C.M. Śrīvāstava (2007); the translator Giri Ratna Mishra (2015); the bazaar-print compilers named on Bṛhat Indrajāla title pages (Rameshwar Mishra, Devcharan Awasthi, 'Ojha Baba'); the Kerala mantravāda ritual families; and the still-operating Khemraj Shrikrishnadas / Gita Press-adjacent trade. Judgements about their work are attributed to the scholar who made them and are never adopted as the slice's own. Ullrey's assessment that one 2015 English translation 'has little to do with the root text' is recorded AS ULLREY'S, with his footnote located.
meta.assertedField: Every edge carries `ASSERTED` as a boolean with a fixed meaning. `true` = this slice asserts the relation holds and `evidence` names the documentation. `false` = the edge is recorded as a CANDIDATE that this slice explicitly DECLINES to assert, and `basis` says why the declination stands. Resemblance edges — shared goddess-lists, shared result-vocabulary, shared genre — are recorded at ASSERTED:false unless a documented dependency exists. This is the field the auditor should attack first.

works.title: The Uḍḍ-corpus (the Uḍḍīśa cluster) — the core Indian grimoire family
works.author: au:anonymous-udd
works.dateText: no securable date; the family is post-medieval in its surviving witnesses, with older palm-leaf attestations in Maithili, Newari and Nandinagari script implying greater age for some members
works.structuralNote: The corpus term is Ullrey's own coinage ('Uḍḍ-corpus'; Goudriaan called the same body the 'Uḍḍīśa cluster'). Membership is NOT established by the title-syllable: Ullrey's stated criterion is a CLUSTER of characteristic opening verses PLUS exposition of the six results PLUS overt concern with pragmatic ritual — 'a cluster of these generic verses identifies an Uḍḍ-corpus text, merely containing a single one does not' (U1 p. 196). The family is held together by 'family resemblances' and explicitly NOT by a 'family tree' of textual development and branching recension (U1 p. 194).

procedures.typeAsFiled: corpus-level: six-results catalogue (ṣaṭkarman) + fantastic feats/enchanted items (kautukakarman, indrajāla) + conjuring (yakṣiṇīsādhana)
procedures.completenessBasis: grading is done per member work below
procedures.evidence: U1's three-part emic definition of Indian tantra magic (p. 185 n.99, restated p. 552): (1) the six acts, (2) conjuring goddesses, (3) fantastic feats and enchanted items. The Uḍḍ-corpus organises its material under all three, which is why it is the corpus's structural centre.
procedures.harmNote: REQUIRED at corpus level — the six results include māraṇa (murderous sorcery) and its sub-class nāśana (destruction), and two of the three published Uḍḍīśatantra recensions open the body of the text with murder rather than with pacification (U1 pp. 184, 187).

contested.flag: Whether the corpus has a locatable ur-text or a derivational stemma.

positions.holder: Goudriaan (1981), as summarised at U1 p. 194 n.118
positions.value: the Uḍḍīśatantra is DERIVED from (1) the Uḍḍāmara/Uḍḍāmareśvara alias Mantracintāmaṇi, (2) the Uḍḍīśatantra alias Rāvaṇoḍḍīśa, (3) the Vīrabhadratantra alias Mantrakośa, and (4) the Kriyoḍḍīśatantra; and the dialogue partner distinguishes members (Śiva-Pārvatī in the Uḍḍāmara/Uḍḍāmareśvara, Śiva-Rāvaṇa in the Uḍḍīśa).

'Frequent back-and-forth borrowing prohibitively complicates any search for an Uḍḍ-corpus ur-text… I have yet to encounter a single, early source that all Uḍḍ-corpus texts — or even most — stem from' (p. 194). And on Goudriaan's criterion: 'dialogue partners often switch in these texts making Goudriaan's argument not consistently valid' (p. 194 n.118).

The attribution is a revelation-frame, not a historical claim, and the dialogue partners switch mid-text between Rāvaṇa and a goddess.
works.structuralNote: ANATOMY, as evidenced from the Tripathī recension (U1 pp. 182-183): the text divides into a first half (pūrvārdha) and later half (uttarārdha). The first half itself has two parts — (i) SYSTEMATIC verses correlating variables to results, then (ii) an ENCYCLOPEDIC catalogue of six-result techniques, sixty-nine verses under eight headings. The later half carries results not classifiable under the six, plus a lore layer: remedies for procedural error, methods of counteracting magic, and recourse when results fail to appear. It closes with fantastic feats and enchanted items, magic slippers, alchemical concoctions and revivification. That closing block is where the text GROWS: 'New material can be easily added to the end of the manuscript' (U1 p. 184).

editions.translator: Śyāmasundaralāla Tripāṭhī (Sanskrit root text + original Hindi commentary)
editions.note: Per its own introduction it REPRODUCES a prior Sanskrit publication issued by order of Seṭh Khemarāj Śrīkṛṣṇadās at the Bombay Veṅkaṭeśvara Steam Press; Ullrey had access to neither that earlier print nor its manuscript (U1 p. 182). Ullrey judges the commentary 'clear, faithful to the root text', with footnotes 'useful, though occasionally erroneous'.

editions.translator: Śivadatta Miśra ('Śivadattī' Hindi commentary), edited from a single manuscript with Paṇḍit Śrī Hīrāmaṇi Miśra
editions.note: Ullrey: 'carefully edited into clear, workaday Sanskrit', with a consistent chapter-and-verse numbering scheme, and an ornate purāṇic Sanskrit introduction setting the revelation on Kailāsa (U1 p. 184).

editions.translator: C.M. Śrīvāstava (Uḍḍīśa Taṃtra Sādhana Evaṃ Prayog — Hindi introductions, commentary, appendices and original chapters)
editions.note: The longest and most recent. Ullrey: the root Sanskrit is 'rough; some verses are unintelligible', riddled with spelling and sandhi errors 'consistent with manuscripts', and printed WITHOUT verse numbers — either reproducing a poor manuscript or copying poorly edited earlier prints (U1 pp. 186-187). Śrīvāstava is described as an AUTHOR rather than a glossator.

procedures.typeAsFiled: six-results catalogue (ṣaṭkarman) — encyclopedic
procedures.completenessBasis: read-through of a scholar who translated the whole recension
procedures.evidence: Ullrey translated Tripathī's Uḍḍīśatantra IN FULL as Appendix One of the dissertation (pp. 644-682), including the six-results catalogue at pp. 661-671. He states his method at p. 146: 'I translate mantras, deity names, ingredients, and procedures in full.' The individual rites therefore carry all three parts a working operation needs — ritual action, mantra, and declared result — and the encyclopedic composition strategy he names first is exactly 'three part discrete verses with mantra, thereby including ritual actions, mantra, and result' (p. 159). Grade 'complete' is asserted for the RITE-LEVEL entries in this recension only, and only because a full translation exists and was made from the printed root text.
procedures.harmNote: REQUIRED. The catalogue's eight headings run pacification, subjugation, immobilization, bewildering, dissension, eradication, attraction, MURDER. Ullrey devotes pp. 318-357 to murderous sorcery (māraṇa) and destruction (nāśana) across the three recensions. Targets are human by default. No rite, mantra, substance, count or timing crosses into this file.

procedures.typeAsFiled: systematic variable-tables (second-order magic lore)
procedures.completenessBasis: verse range located and its variable-set enumerated by the reading scholar
procedures.evidence: U1 p. 160 locates the systematic block at Tripathī 1.14-163 and enumerates the variable axes: directions faced, times of day, season, days of the week, astrological conjunctions and signs, elements, deity colours and stances, syllables and syllable placement, mantra-language gender, mat markings and materials, hand gestures, visualised deity actions, shape and orientation of offering pits, pot materials, rosary bead and thread materials, fingers used on the rosary, methods of repetition, oblation materials, flame names, and ladle shapes and lengths. The AXES are recorded here; none of their VALUES is.
procedures.harmNote: The same variable tables serve hostile results; that is the point of a systematic tantra.

procedures.typeAsFiled: error-remedy and counter-magic lore (procedural failure handling)
procedures.completenessBasis: the section is located and characterised, but its internal completeness was not assessed by any source read
procedures.evidence: U1 p. 157 n.32 places this in the later half, verses 2.1-89 — 'sequences of results to be performed if results are not apparent… signs of perfection (siddhilakṣaṇa), ranking of perfections, symptomatology of afflictions (doṣa) caused by magic… and lore for bestowing faults and gaining fruits.' Graded 'partial' because Ullrey characterises the topics but the dissertation does not test whether the section is internally step-complete, and this slice did not read the appendix translation of the later half.
procedures.harmNote: Counter-magic (defensive) and affliction-symptomatology sit in the same block as the offensive lore — the corpus does not separate them.

procedures.typeAsFiled: fantastic feats and enchanted items (kautuhalakarman, indrajāla), including alchemical concoctions and revivification claims
procedures.completenessBasis: named as present and as an accretion zone; contents not assessed
procedures.evidence: U1 p. 183 lists the closing topics by name (magic slippers / pādukāsādhana, guṭikā and rasāyana concoctions, mṛtasañjīvanī-vidyā) and immediately characterises the block as the site of textual growth: 'Lists of fantastic feats and enchanted items are used by authors to expand texts.' A block whose function is to absorb accretion cannot be graded complete.

contested.flag: The index-verse / contents mismatch — is it error or genre?

positions.value: It is a FORMAL FEATURE of the genre, not a defect: 'Index verses differing from actual contents of the text is common, if not universal, in magic tantras' (p. 183 n.95); 'Index lists, in fact, rarely present a text's contents accurately' (p. 148). All three recensions print a six-item index verse; Tripathī's body gives eight results, Śivadatta's and Śrīvāstava's give seven, in three different orders.

contested.note: Recorded as contested because no second scholar was read on it. It is the single most useful diagnostic in the slice: a text whose own table of contents does not match its body cannot be graded from its index verse.

contested.flag: Manuscript provenance of the three printed recensions.

positions.value: 'Manuscript provenance is undetermined; publishers, editors, and commentators leave unspecified — or they only elliptically describe — their sources. I have not identified manuscript attestations, though I have recognized verses from all three texts in Uḍḍ-corpus manuscripts' (p. 181). Śivadatta's and Śrīvāstava's sources are 'likely located in Varanasi'; Śrīvāstava 'may not have consulted manuscripts at all but copied poorly edited published editions' (p. 186).

Nothing operative is reproduced here.

A source-claim in this corpus is a genre gesture, not a citation.

procedures.typeAsFiled: unassessed — the work is known to this slice only as a cited source-name

works.titleOriginal: असली प्राचीन रावण संहिता — Asalī prācīna Rāvaṇa saṃhitā ('The Genuine Ancient Rāvaṇa Saṃhitā')
works.author: au:ravana-pseudepigraphic

works.attributionNote: Attributed to Rāvaṇa. The title functions as a marketing frame that gathers heterogeneous material under one demon-king brand; the 'asalī prācīna' ('genuine ancient') in the title is itself a trade signal that competing prints exist.
works.structuralNote: ANATOMY OF A BAZAAR OMNIBUS, per U1 p. 182 n.93. Six sections: (1) an account of Rāvaṇa's life; (2) prognostication by planets and signs; (3) prognostication by stars and asterisms; (4) the Uḍḍīśatantra 'composed by Rāvaṇa'; (5) the Kriyoḍḍīśatantra as a Śiva–Pārvatī dialogue; (6) a discourse on male erotics ascribed to Rāvaṇa, closing with a Śiva hymn. Astrology, grimoire and sex manual bound as one commodity — the Indian counterpart of the composite chapbook. CRUCIAL FINDING: the Uḍḍīśatantra printed here 'is identical to Tripathī's Uḍḍīśatantra' (U1, same note). The omnibus is a re-wrapper of an existing print, not an independent witness.

works.title: Bhūtaḍāmaratantra — the BUDDHIST recension ('The Ghost-Hooligan Tantra')
works.titleOriginal: भूतडामरतन्त्र; Tib. 'byung po 'dul byed kyi rgyud (Toh 747)
works.author: au:anonymous-buddhist-bhutadamara
works.dateText: CONTESTED — see contested[]. Bhattacharyya: first part of the 7th c.; 84000's summary: 'around the seventh or eighth century CE'; Ullrey: 'far from secure'.
works.dedupWith: repo abhichara-data.js TEXTS[8] 'Bhūtaḍāmaratantra', date 'early', edition '—', note 'A Buddhist conjuring source feeding the later Uḍḍīśa material.' This row CORRECTS that record on two counts: (1) it does not distinguish the Buddhist from the Śaiva recension, and the distinction is the whole story; (2) the phrase 'feeding the later Uḍḍīśa material' asserts a transmission the cited source does NOT support — see the ASSERTED:false edge gri:bhutadamara-buddhist → gri:udd-corpus. What Ullrey actually says is that goddess-lists are shared, and in the same breath he warns that goddess lists 'must be used with great care since they are not standard, contain both real and fanciful names, and often represent borrowed materials with no semantic value' (p. 562 + n.22).
works.attributionNote: Anonymous. The title-word 'bhūtaḍāmara' is NOT the name of a deity in the text: 'The term bhūtaḍāmara is only found in titles, colophons, and opening narratives; it is not found in the main body of the text' (U1 p. 563). The presiding figure is Vajradhara/Vajrapāṇi/Mahākrodha. A Bhūtaḍāmara DEITY exists outside the tantra, in the Sādhanamālā, as a tantric form of Vajrapāṇi in Akṣobhya's clan (U1 pp. 563-564, citing Bhattacharyya 1968).
works.structuralNote: ANATOMY. (1) A frame narrative in which Vajradhara/Vajrapāṇi subjugates Maheśvara, forcing the Śaiva god to convert and to protect those who practise the text's rites — the text's warrant for commanding what it commands. (2) Sequences of named female spirit-classes, each list headed by a chief entity, each list followed by its own corresponding mantras, hand-gestures and ritual exertions. (3) A discrete Vajradhara maṇḍala whose practice conjures and subjugates a wide range of beings. (4) A kiṃkara ('servitor') section that makes Hindu gods into slaves. (5) A closing discourse on multiple emptinesses (śūnya) with no doctrinal exposition attached. ORGANISING PRINCIPLE: not by result, as in the Uḍḍ-corpus, but by SPIRIT PANTHEON — 'techniques… are presented based on spirit pantheons in a loose, over-arching maṇḍala of being, ranging from dryads (yakṣiṇī) to demons (bhūtinī) to snakes (nāginī)' (U1 p. 552). Prose, not verse. Mantras written out plainly rather than encoded.

editions.translator: Aaron Michael Ullrey — 'somewhat-critical' partial edition from Nepali (Newari-script) manuscripts, Appendix Three of the 2016 dissertation
editions.note: Ullrey states he was 'preparing a full critical edition and translation of the Buddhist version' (p. 553 n.2); whether that ever appeared was NOT checked this round. Principal manuscripts named: NAK C-0027-03 (palm-leaf, incomplete, oldest), A-0141-06 (oldest complete, paper), A-0140-10 (closest to the Tibetan), with E-0700-19 and E-2329-04 later.

The 84000 reading-room pages are client-side rendered and returned no body text to two fetch attempts this round; the introduction, chapter list and text were NOT READ. Everything attributed to 84000 here comes from landing-page metadata and a search-result summary and is flagged as such.

editions.note: The 1933 article tabulated the Buddhist and Śaiva chapter contents side by side. Ullrey: it 'has yet to be surpassed' (p. 548). Bhattacharyya worked from a Baroda Oriental Institute copy he judged 'a recent copy of some older manuscript… as found in Nepal very probably in the Durbar Library' (quoted U1 p. 554).

procedures.typeAsFiled: spirit-compelling / conjuring (bhūtinī- and yakṣiṇī-sādhana) with a named hierarchy
procedures.completenessBasis: a first sādhana was edited and translated in full by a reader of the manuscripts, and the remainder characterised as repetitive variants of it
procedures.evidence: Ullrey edited and translated the first complete sādhana — the one immediately following the frame narrative — and then states: 'Subsequent rituals are repetitive; consequently, I shift from detailed translation to paraphrase in sections following this one' (p. 575). The rite as he prints it carries every part an operation needs: named target-spirit, mantra with a name-slot, a stated repetition regime, a ritual site, offerings, and a declared outcome, plus eight indexed variations matched to the eight Demon Princesses. Grade 'complete' is asserted at the RITE level for this sādhana and its variant set. NONE of the mantra, count, site-preparation or offering detail is reproduced in this file.
procedures.harmNote: REQUIRED, and severe on two axes. (a) COERCIVE SANCTION: the compelling procedure carries an explicit clause that if the summoned spirit does not appear, she is destroyed; and non-serving spirits are killed by the presiding deity (U1 pp. 575-576). (b) SERVITOR/SEXUAL OUTCOME: the declared results include enslavement (kiṃkarī) and, in the first variation, sexual compliance. This is recorded as what the text SAYS. The named hierarchy is not reproduced beyond the fact of its existence and its size; nothing here can be executed.

procedures.typeAsFiled: mudrā-based compelling (hand-gesture repertoire attached to the spirit-classes)
procedures.completenessBasis: the FUNCTION-SET is enumerated by the reading scholar, who deliberately withheld the gesture descriptions at that point in his own text
procedures.evidence: U1 pp. 575-576 enumerates what the gesture set is FOR — drawing the spirit forth, binding her to the practitioner's will, subjugating her, calling her from a distance, casting her in any direction, forcing an action, and striking her — and then says 'I will not describe the specific mudrā practice here.' The function-list survives; the executable content does not, in his text or in this one. Graded 'partial' because the source read does not establish whether the tantra's own gesture descriptions are step-complete.
procedures.harmNote: The function-set is a coercion vocabulary: summon, bind, subjugate, compel, strike.

procedures.typeAsFiled: maṇḍala practice (Vajradhara/Mahākrodha), including initiation and mantra-being material
procedures.completenessBasis: sections located by heading in a scholar's chapter outline; contents not assessed here
procedures.evidence: U1's chapter-seven headings locate 'Vajradhara's Dominating Maṇḍala' (p. 589), 'Mantras, Mantra Beings, and Initiation' (p. 595) and 'Maṇḍala Results and Conjuring Vajradhara' (p. 597). This slice read the surrounding argument, not those pages; the grade reflects that.
procedures.harmNote: The maṇḍala's declared function is to conjure and subjugate 'a wide range of powerful creatures' (U1 p. 552).

procedures.typeAsFiled: subjugation of rival-tradition deities (kiṃkara-sādhana — 'making Hindu gods into slaves')
procedures.completenessBasis: section located and its polemical function established; contents not read
procedures.evidence: U1 p. 600 heading, and the argument at pp. 556-557: the Buddhist text 'treats Hindu deities as demons and world protectors', and retains 'subjugation and murder rituals against high Hindu gods, unheard of in an originally Hindu tantra'. This is the load-bearing evidence for the recension-priority argument, so its presence is well attested even though its procedures were not read.
procedures.harmNote: Inter-traditional polemic executed as ritual violence against another community's gods. Recorded as religious history; no content reproduced. This is material a modern reader may find offensive to a living tradition, and it is presented as what a medieval text does, not as a verdict on Buddhism or Śaivism.

procedures.typeAsFiled: dismissal / release of the compelled spirit (visarjana)
procedures.completenessBasis: attested for the ritual grammar, NOT located as a rubric inside this text — see the honesty note
procedures.evidence: HONESTY NOTE, and the auditor should press here. Ullrey observes that the tantra's compelling-gesture results 'echo the five-fold ritual sequences found elsewhere: invocation, depositing, gaining attention, worship, and dismissal' (p. 576). But his footnote for that five-fold sequence cites the JAIN Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa 3.24, not the Bhūtaḍāmaratantra. So: the five-part sequence terminating in visarjana is documented for the surrounding ritual grammar of the magic tantras; an analyst reads the Bhūtaḍāmara's gesture-set as echoing it; and NO source read this round places a dismissal rubric inside the Bhūtaḍāmaratantra itself. Grade 'referenced' means exactly that and no more. This matters because the licence-to-depart is the single most-cited structural point of comparison with the Ars Goetia, and it is the weakest link in that comparison as the evidence currently stands.

contested.flag: Priority: is the Buddhist recension earlier than the Śaiva one?

positions.holder: Bhattacharyya (1933), as reported at U1 pp. 548-557
positions.value: YES — the Buddhist version is prior; and further, the tantra-age deities involved (Kālī, Tārā, Bhadrakālī, Sarasvatī, Mañjughoṣa, Chinnamastā) were 'originally Buddhist' and were folded into the Śaiva system by Hindus attracted to their power and adaptability.

YES on priority — 'The tantra's earliest form is Buddhist, but it was re-written, simplified, and then expanded to become a Śaiva text' (p. 565) — but NO on Bhattacharyya's deity claim: 'I find the assertion that Sarasvatī was originally Buddhist to be patently false. Tārā and Mañjughoṣa seem to be likely Buddhist. Kāli and Bhadrakālī appear to arise in a fluid world neither Hindu or Buddhist' (p. 553 n.3). Ullrey also flags Bhattacharyya's 'Buddhist chauvinism… obvious though of a piece with his time of writing', while granting that here 'that bias is supported by data'.

positions.holder: Sanderson (2009), as reported at U1 p. 565 n.29
positions.value: The GENERAL direction of borrowing is Śaiva → Buddhist; Buddhists adopted and intensified Śaiva ritual technology. Ullrey accepts this as the rule and treats the Bhūtaḍāmara as a documented REVERSAL of it: 'while the direction was usually Śaiva to Buddhist, the direction is reversed here.' Why the Śaivas took up this particular Buddhist text 'remains a mystery'.
Buddhist version: first part of the 7th century.

positions.holder: P. Pal (1981), as cited at U1 p. 564 n.26 — Ullrey states he has not consulted Pal
positions.value: Hindu version: between the 11th and 15th centuries.
compiled anonymously around the 7th or 8th century CE.
'These dates are far from secure' (p. 564).

contested.flag: Whether the text belongs to a Tibetan doxographic class (kriyā/caryā/yoga/anuttarayoga).

works.title: Bhūtaḍāmaratantra — the ŚAIVA recension
works.author: au:anonymous-saiva-bhutadamara
works.dateText: later than the Buddhist recension and later than the Tibetan translation of it; Pal's 11th-15th c. range is the only figure on offer and Ullrey did not consult Pal. Earliest DATED Śaiva manuscript Ullrey found: T23-4, 1762, Devanāgarī — with undated Newari- and Maithili-script copies that 'appear older'.
works.attributionNote: Framed as a dialogue between Unmattabhairava and his consort. The Buddhist conversion narrative is gone entirely: 'The Śaiva text has no conversion narrative whatsoever' (U1 p. 567).
works.structuralNote: ANATOMY, and the reason this recension matters formally. Bhattacharyya's side-by-side chapter table showed the Śaiva text incorporating and augmenting the Buddhist one. Ullrey's summary of the difference is the slice's best single formal marker: 'the Śaiva text is systematic, the Buddhist encyclopedic' (p. 553). Concretely, the Śaiva recension (a) establishes consistent deity lists, (b) imposes a coherent structure with matching colophons, (c) applies a mantra-CODE system (mantroddhāra / mantrakośa) across the whole text, and (d) is written in VERSE where the Buddhist is prose. Buddhist material is retained undigested: goddess-lists and female-deity cycles survive, Buddhist worship-sites survive in place-names, and Buddhist deity names survive inside the mantras. Overt Buddhist doctrine (the closing śūnya discourse) is removed. Catalogue records give a paṭala 1-15 structure for Śaiva witnesses.

editions.translator: — no critical edition located
editions.note: HONEST GAP. Ullrey collected 26 Śaiva manuscripts from the National Archives, Kathmandu alone, and reports the recension throughout Indian archives; no critical edition of the Śaiva recension was located this round. Devotional/trade prints exist (an English-language 'Bhuta Damara Tantra… of Sri Krodha Bhairava' is sold commercially) and are NOT scholarship.

procedures.typeAsFiled: spirit-compelling / conjuring, systematised (bhūtinī cycles with regularised names)
procedures.completenessBasis: the recension's relationship to a translated rite is documented, but the recension itself has no edition and was not read
procedures.evidence: U1 p. 575 n.50: the third chapter of the Śaiva version 'reproduces this sādhana in an expanded, simplified, and more systematic form. In general, the Hindu version resolves ambiguity of techniques but encodes the mantras.' The bhūtinī names are regularised — 'pressed into more palatable, pleasant Sanskrit titles' — and are 'explicitly matched up in sequence with the specific rituals'. So the rite is MORE explicit procedurally and LESS explicit mantrically than its Buddhist parent. Cannot be graded 'complete': no edition exists and nobody read the whole.
procedures.harmNote: Inherits the Buddhist recension's compelling logic and adds it to a Śaiva frame. It ALSO retains 'subjugation and murder rituals against high Hindu gods' — which is the anomaly on which the priority argument turns (U1 p. 557).

procedures.typeAsFiled: mantra-encoding apparatus (mantroddhāra / mantrakośa) — a deliberate withholding device
procedures.textCompleteness: complete-as-a-device, and DELIBERATELY INCOMPLETE as transmission
procedures.completenessBasis: the withholding is the finding, and it is documented twice over
procedures.evidence: THE SLICE'S KEY WITHHOLDING FINDING. 'The Śaiva version presents coded mantras (mantroddhāra); mantras are uncoded in the Buddhist text and are written exactly as to be spoken. In general, earlier tantras portray explicit mantras and later ones use mantra codes; consequently, coded mantras indicate posteriority' (U1 p. 565). A mantra-code substitutes descriptive epithets for syllables, so that the operative core is retrievable only by a reader who already holds the key — i.e. an initiate. This is a text that is complete as an artefact and unusable as a manual by design. It also gives philology a DATING TOOL: encoding correlates with lateness. The repo should record this as the Indian corpus's own answer to the question the Western grimoire tradition answers with cipher and notarikon.
procedures.harmNote: The encoding does not reduce the harm profile; it restricts the audience.

works.title: The Ḍāmara family (ḍāmaratantras) — a long-standing native genre label
works.author: au:various
works.dateText: undated as a family
works.structuralNote: 'ḍāmara is a long-standing tantra categorization' (U1 p. 191) — that is, an EMIC genre term, not a modern scholarly grouping. The Dattātreyatantra names a group of ḍāmaratantras and counts the Uḍḍīśatantra among them (U1 p. 191 n.114), which is the corpus's own testimony that the Uḍḍ- and Ḍāmara- labels overlap. Monier-Williams lists six titled members: Yogaḍāmara, Śivaḍāmara, Durgāḍāmara, Sārasvataḍāmara, Brahmaḍāmara, Gandharvaḍāmara (via U1 p. 565 n.27). The word is Śiva's noisy drum (ḍamaru); Sanderson's suggested English is 'hooligan'.

procedures.typeAsFiled: family label covering operative tantras generally
procedures.completenessBasis: no member text was examined this round beyond the Bhūtaḍāmara pair
procedures.evidence: The family is recorded because the corpus itself uses the label and because the label is a live source of confusion — see contested[].

contested.flag: Whether the Bhūtaḍāmaratantra belongs to the Ḍāmara family. THE SLICE'S MOST IMPORTANT NEGATIVE FINDING.

positions.value: NO, twice over. 'The Bhūtaḍāmaratantra should not be confused with Śaiva Ḍāmaratantras to which the Bhūtaḍamaratantra has no connection' (p. 565), and 'This text is not directly connected to the so-called Ḍāmara tantras of any variety or the east Indian Ḍāmarutantra' (p. 565); the footnote adds that 'Publications of the simply named Ḍāmaratantra should not be grouped with the Buddhist or Hindu Bhūtaḍāmaratantra' (n.27).

positions.holder: The title-syllable, and any classification built on it
positions.value: would group them.

contested.note: Recorded as contested only because a name-based grouping is the default error; Ullrey's position is the only sourced one and this slice follows it. Any future edge joining gri:bhutadamara-* to gri:damara-family must be ASSERTED:false.

works.title: The east Indian Ḍāmarutantra (the 'Bangla Damaru')

works.structuralNote: Composed in hybrid Sanskrit and Bengali, it reproduces both common rituals and whole goddess/spirit cycles from the Bhūtaḍāmaratantra. This is the slice's clearest case of an operative Sanskrit text passing INTO a regional vernacular manual.

editions.translator: — none located

procedures.typeAsFiled: spirit-cycle conjuring, vernacularised
procedures.completenessBasis: the whole record rests on a table of contents and two conversations reported at second hand
procedures.evidence: EVIDENCE IS THIN AND THE THINNESS IS THE POINT. U1 p. 566 n.30 in full substance: Keith Cantú translated the table of contents; from that table and 'several conversations with Cantú', Ullrey observed shared rituals with the Śaiva (and ultimately Buddhist) Bhūtaḍāmaratantra plus 'reproductions of goddess/spirit cycles… in the Bengali source'. No edition, no manuscript shelfmark, no published study. A search this round for Cantú on the Ḍāmara material returned nothing — his published work is on Bengali Sufism, the Yoga Kalandar and Bāul Fakiri song. So the ONLY evidence for this work is a personal communication reported in a footnote.
procedures.harmNote: Presumed to share the compelling logic of its source; NOT verified.

works.title: Kakṣapuṭa (Siddhanāgārjunakakṣapuṭa; also Kacchapuṭa)
works.author: au:nagarjuna-siddha-attributed
works.dateText: c. 10th c. by common attribution; no critical dating located this round
works.attributionNote: ATTRIBUTED TO SIDDHA NĀGĀRJUNA — and this is a three-way conflation the repo already polices. (1) The 2nd-c. Madhyamaka philosopher Nāgārjuna: a DIFFERENT person, already a separate node in the repo at confluence.js 'Nāgārjuna (Madhyamaka philosopher)'. (2) The Siddha/alchemical Nāgārjuna: the repo's confluence.js 'Nagarjuna the alchemist' carries a contested block with both positions, and rasa-data.js encodes Wujastyk's finding that 'the Rasaratnākara by Nāgārjuna' is a manuscript-conflation GHOST (the genuine works being the Rasendramaṅgala of Nāgārjuna Siddha and the Rasaratnākara of Nityanātha Siddha). (3) A third use the operative corpus adds: 'Nāgārjuna' as a BAZAAR-PRINT AUTHOR-BRAND. Ullrey's bibliography carries an Āścaryayogamālātantra ascribed to 'the perennial author Nāgārjuna', ed. Baladevaprasāda Miśra, published by Khemarāja Śrīkṛṣṇadāsa (Bombay, 2005 printing) — and he adds a footnote 'On the many Nāgārjunas in Hinduism' (U1 p. 1023-1024 of the extract's line numbering; dissertation bibliography). This slice asserts NO identification among the three and re-confuses none of them. NOTE for the repo: rasa-data.js already cites the Kakṣapuṭa for Nāgārjuna's 4×4 magic-square construction method — so the repo ALREADY holds a Kakṣapuṭa datum, filed under alchemy, without knowing the text is a ṣaṭkarman grimoire.
works.structuralNote: Encyclopedic in Ullrey's sense, and the most systematised of the five texts printed in the 1915 Indrajālavidyāsaṃgraha — 'The Siddhanāgārjunakakṣapuṭam is the longest and most systematized' (U1 p. 117 n.24). Content includes six-results operations (ṣaṭkarman), a yakṣiṇī-mantra-sādhana block ('invoking yakṣiṇīs'), and ceṭaka practices ('using as a slave'). It is also where the term indrajāla appears as a SIDDHI — a supernatural power — rather than as a genre label.

editions.translator: printed in the Indrajālavidyāsaṃgraha (Calcutta, 1915) as one of five texts
editions.quoteSafe: PD, but this round quotes nothing — and the edition is uncritical (see gri:indrajalavidyasamgraha)

works.title: Indrajālavidyāsaṃgraha — the 1915 Calcutta magic-anthology
works.author: au:various
works.dateText: 1915 (the anthology); its five constituent texts are of unrelated dates and provenances
works.structuralNote: THE CORPUS'S MOST CONSEQUENTIAL EDITORIAL ACCIDENT. Five texts printed together: Indrajālaśāstra, Kāmaratna, Dattātreyatantra, Ṣaṭkarmadīpikā, and Siddhanāgārjunakakṣapuṭa. Ullrey's verdict on the grouping is blunt: none of the five 'are organically connected by a religious tradition, common source, or geographic area… These tantras are only connected by appearing in the same publication' (pp. 116-117). Manuscript sources were collected from eastern India and printed WITHOUT emendation — Goudriaan's own description, quoted by Ullrey, calls the result 'uncritical, without adequate numbering of stanzas, without introductory comment by the editors, and without any warning that in some places the material is incomplete, perhaps because of deliberate omission by the editors' (U1 p. 116 n.22). Ullrey's comparison of the volume's Dattātreyatantra against Kathmandu manuscripts found 'great similarity in content and organization but substantial differences within the verses'.

editions.translator: editorship UNRESOLVED — see U8 discrepancy
editions.quoteSafe: PD, but the edition is uncritical and its text is not a reliable witness; this round quotes nothing
editions.note: The archive.org scan (CC0 by uploader) files it under the 'Complete Works of Jibananda Vidyasagara'; search results give the editors as Aśubodha Vidyābhūṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya and Nityabodha Vidyāratna Bhaṭṭācārya. Ullrey names no editor. UNRESOLVED — do not print an editor without saying which record it came from.

procedures.typeAsFiled: anthology-level: ṣaṭkarman + indrajāla + conjuring + erotics + toxicology
procedures.completenessBasis: the volume is documented as possibly carrying DELIBERATE editorial omissions, which is itself a completeness finding
procedures.evidence: Goudriaan (quoted U1 p. 116 n.22) suspects 'deliberate omission by the editors'. Ullrey partly demurs — 'Deliberate omissions by the editors are possible, as Goudriaan suggests, but omissions and inclusions occur regularly during textual transmission' (p. 117 n.23) — and adds that these texts 'contain awkward seams where material is inserted or tacked on artlessly and without citation; such seams may appear to be sites of omission but instead are signals of continual accretion.' Either way the volume cannot be graded complete, and the two competing explanations for its gaps are both recorded.
procedures.harmNote: REQUIRED at the volume level — it contains at least two ṣaṭkarman texts.

contested.flag: Why these five texts were printed together.

positions.value: 'Likely, the texts were published together because of their common concern with magic and alchemy and Śaiva orientation. We cannot discount that they were published together because a trove of manuscripts was discovered that just happened to include these texts' (p. 116 n.22).

contested.note: This matters because Goudriaan built a 'classic' ṣaṭkarman list partly on this volume's contents, and Ullrey's counter is that the anthology's boundaries are an accident of publication being read as a tradition: he proposes Goudriaan's study 'would be more accurately titled A Study of the Six Acts in the Indrajālavidyāsaṃgraha with Selected References to Other Tantras, as Inspired by Passages in the Mahāmāyā Fragment' (p. 117 n.22).

works.author: au:anonymous-indrajala

The word indrajāla covers both a genre ('fantastic feats and enchanted items', kautuhalakarman) and, in the Kakṣapuṭa, a siddhi. Ullrey treats indrajāla as the SECOND of the three emic constituents of Indian tantra magic.

editions.note: no independent edition located

works.title: Bṛhat Indrajāla / Bṛhad Indrajāl — a bazaar title with no critical existence
works.author: au:bazaar-compilers
works.dateText: modern; the circulating compilations are 20th-21st c. and undated on their title pages
works.structuralNote: THE ROW THE SLICE IS LEAST WILLING TO DRESS UP. What can be established: the title circulates in at least three mutually independent modern compilations under different named compilers and different publishers — a Khemraj Prakashan edition attributed to Pt. Devcharan Awasthi; a DPB Publication edition attributed to Pt. Rameshwar Mishra; a Deep Prakashan 'Prāchīn Bṛhat Indrajāl' attributed to 'Ojha Baba'; plus English-language repackagings. That is ALL that is established.

Pt. Rameshwar Mishra (attrib., comp.)
'Ojha Baba' (attrib.), as Prāchīn Bṛhat Indrajāl

procedures.typeAsFiled: mixed ṣaṭkarman results (subjugation, bewildering, eradication) under an indrajāla title
procedures.completenessBasis: NO SCHOLARSHIP EXISTS THAT THIS SLICE COULD LOCATE, and no completeness grade is offered

There is no critical edition, no manuscript study, no academic treatment, and no way from the evidence available to say whether the constituent rites are step-complete, abridged, or invented for the print. Recording 'no grade' is the honest output; recording a grade from a bookseller's blurb would be exactly the failure the brief warns against — 'dressing up a bazaar print as a source'.

works.title: Kāmaratna / Kāmaratnatantra
works.author: au:nityanatha-attributed
works.dateText: undated; the Assamese/Kāmākhyā association is a provenance claim, not a date

NOTE the repo-relevant trap: Nityanātha Siddha is the genuine author of the Rasaratnākara per Wujastyk 1984 (already encoded at rasa-data.js). Whether the Kāmaratna's 'Nityanātha' is the same figure was NOT established this round and MUST NOT be assumed.

The 1899 Bombay print runs 370 pages with a 27-page appendix of yantra plates; the 1928 Shillong edition runs 110 pages with 20 pages of diagrams. THOSE TWO OBJECTS ARE NOT THE SAME TEXT AT THE SAME LENGTH, and no source read this round reconciles them.

procedures.completenessBasis: characterised by Goudriaan at category level; no reader of a full edition consulted

procedures.harmNote: Erotic-compulsion material in this corpus is continuous with vaśīkaraṇa. Recorded, not detailed.

procedures.typeAsFiled: 'mechanical' mantra-rites — rites with no presiding deity and no invocation
procedures.completenessBasis: a live methodological dispute about this very text, recorded rather than resolved
procedures.evidence: THE SLICE'S BEST STRUCTURAL DISPUTE. Goudriaan called some Kāmaratna recipes 'automatic' — 'the mantra must have been thought to work automatically' — because they carry no deity name and no presiding deity. Ullrey rejects the term while keeping the category: 'these rituals are not automatic because they require actions — intentional actions that are often quite long and intense. Merely removing a deity name from a mantra, according to Goudriaan, would thereby make the whole ritual automatic… Throughout the magic tantras I have seen the exact same rituals used with a mantra and without a mantra, the rituals are not made automatic as much as the deity-component is added or removed. The ritual performed without invocation is thereby MECHANICAL — it is effective based on its inherent power and its perfect performance' (U1 p. 154 n.29). Both positions are recorded. The distinction matters for the Western comparison: a mechanical rite has no spirit to bind and therefore no licence to depart.

procedures.completenessBasis: listed under a heading by Goudriaan; not examined

works.title: Dattātreyatantra

works.title: Tantrasamuccaya of Cennas Nārāyaṇan Nambūtiri
works.author: au:cennas-narayanan-nambutiri
works.dateText: 15th c.; commonly given as 1427-28 CE, composed under the Sāmūtiri (Zamorin) polity
works.structuralNote: THE SLICE'S MOST IMPORTANT CORRECTIVE TO ITS OWN BRIEF. The Tantrasamuccaya is Kerala's dominant ritual manual — but it is a TEMPLE manual, not a grimoire. Its subject is temple ritual from the construction of a new temple through installation (pratiṣṭhā) to expiatory procedure (prāyaścitta); it remains the working reference for temple architecture and ritual in Kerala today. It is a paddhati — a sequenced liturgical handbook — and paddhati completeness is a DIFFERENT axis from grimoire completeness: a paddhati is complete when a qualified officiant can run the liturgy, which is precisely the property that makes it non-transferable to an outsider. Filing it under 'operative manual literature' because it is called a tantra would be the same category error as filing the Ars Notoria under conjuration. It earns its place in this slice for a different reason: it is the DIVIDING LINE of the Kerala corpus. Syamkumar periodises the literature into a 'Pre-Tantrasamuccaya phase' emphasising philosophical and mythological dimensions and a 'Post-Tantrasamuccaya phase' whose manuals 'mainly concentrate only on the practical side of Tantric rituals'.

editions.translator: T. Ganapati Sastri (Sanskrit text with Śaṅkara's Vimarśinī commentary)

works.title: Tantrasārasaṃgraha of Nārāyaṇa (the Viṣanārāyaṇīya) — the Kerala operative manual proper
works.author: au:narayana-sivapura
works.dateText: 15th-16th c.; a Kerala brahmin resident at Śivapura on the Nila river
works.structuralNote: THIS — not the Tantrasamuccaya — is the Kerala corpus's operative manual, and the slice's answer to where Kerala mantravāda actually lives in Sanskrit. 32 chapters, c. 2,100 verses besides the mantra portions. The FIRST TEN CHAPTERS are viṣavaidya, toxicology — mantra-treatment of poison and snakebite, which is why the text is popularly named after poison rather than after tantra. The remaining chapters cover grahapīḍā (affliction by seizing spirits/planets), kṣudra-dhvaṃsa (destruction of hostile petty magic — i.e. COUNTER-sorcery), unmāda (madness), and kāmika-karma (desire-directed acts). Commentary: Mantravimarśinī of Svarṇagrāma Vāsudeva. NOTE THE SHAPE OF THE HARM PROFILE: a Kerala mantravāda manual is organised around DEFENCE — poison, possession, madness, counter-sorcery — with the desire-directed acts as one heading among several. That is a different distribution from the Uḍḍ-corpus, where murder heads the body-text, and the difference should not be flattened.

editions.translator: N.V.P. Unithiri (ed.), Sanskrit text with the Mantravimarśinī of Svarṇagrāma Vāsudeva, 2 vols

procedures.completenessBasis: chapter allocation documented; contents not read

procedures.harmNote: Toxicology in this tradition is treatment-facing; but a text that maps poisons is also a text that maps poisons. Flagged, not detailed.

works.title: The Kerala mantravāda corpus and the Malayalam manual tradition
works.author: au:various
works.dateText: living tradition on a Sanskrit base of the 11th-16th c.
works.structuralNote: SCHOLARSHIP HERE IS THIN AND THE SLICE SAYS SO. What is established: a Sanskrit operative layer (Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati Mantrapāda; Tantrasārasaṃgraha) distinct from the temple-liturgy paddhatis; a corpus periodisation around the Tantrasamuccaya; named commentators (Trivikrama, Śaṅkara, Nārāyaṇaśiṣya, Svarṇagrāma Vāsudeva); and the practice's transmission through specific Nambūtiri households holding it as family competence. What could NOT be established this round: any scholarly treatment of the MALAYALAM manual tradition as such; the contents of named Malayalam manuals; or any critical edition of a vernacular Kerala mantravāda text. Searches returned temple-history and community-history pages, not scholarship. Two named Kerala items surfaced in the brief and in aggregator lists but were NOT verifiable and are recorded as unverified leads: 'Śeṣasamuccaya' (attrib. Kṛṣṇa Śarma) and the Malayalam household compendium usually called 'Kuzhikkāṭṭu Pacca'.

procedures.typeAsFiled: mantravāda — the Kerala practitioner tradition
procedures.completenessBasis: no vernacular manual was located in an edition or a study
procedures.evidence: Explicit gap. The Sanskrit layer is graded at gri:tantrasarasamgraha and tan:isanasivagurudevapaddhati; the Malayalam layer carries no grade because no evidence was obtained.
procedures.harmNote: REQUIRED at corpus level — mantravāda covers both counter-affliction work and hostile work, and the boundary is drawn by practitioners, not by the texts.

contested.flag: How Kerala practitioners themselves handle the hostile results.

positions.holder: A Nambūtiri tantrika interviewed by Ullrey in Kerala, reported at U1 p. 189 n.108
positions.value: Substitution and restriction. In his practice dangerous offerings are replaced with benign ones, and 'the hostile ritual results are only used against noncorporeal malignant creatures, demons and the like'. He stressed 'the power of mantra over ritual', cited the mantras in his FAMILY tantras as the source of his power, and 'had no interest in traditional or literal performance of the rituals in his family tantras'.

reads this as a Kerala instance of a general interpretive move — 'all religious groups dress-up grubby grievous grimoires' (p. 188) — the same move he documents for Buddhist hermeneuts and Jain 'soft murder'.

contested.note: This is a single interview with one living practitioner, reported in a footnote. It is recorded because it is the only first-hand Kerala testimony obtained, and it is NOT generalised to Kerala practice. The slice takes no position on whether the substitution account is descriptive, normative, or offered to a visiting researcher.

works.title: The printed-bazaar tantra-mantra trade — where the living tradition meets print
works.author: au:various
works.dateText: 1868-present; the formative phase c. 1871-1930
works.structuralNote: THE SLICE'S CENTRAL CLAIM ABOUT TRANSMISSION, and the answer to 'how did this actually circulate'. Almost nothing in the Indian grimoire corpus reaches a modern reader through a critical edition. It reaches them through cheap commercial print, and the houses are nameable. THE PRESS: two Marwari brothers from Churu — Gangavishnu Bajaj and Khemraj Bajaj, sons of Shrikrishnadas — arrive in Mumbai in 1868; Khemraj works as an itinerant bookseller before opening a small press at Moti Bazar in 1871; by 1880 they are at Khetwadi as the Sri Venkateswar Steam Press; the brothers separate in 1893; Gangavishnu having no descendants, Khemraj's line inherits, producing the Khemraj Shrikrishnadas imprint (U12 — TERTIARY, flagged). THE EVIDENCE THAT THIS IS THE OPERATIVE CORPUS'S ACTUAL CHANNEL, and it is direct: (1) the Kāmaratnam of 1899 — 370 pp., Sanskrit with Hindi, 27 pp. of yantra plates — was issued by Khemarāja Śrīkṛṣṇadāsa at Bombay; (2) the Sanskrit Uḍḍīśatantra that Tripathī reproduces was 'published by order of Seṭh Khemarāj Śrīkṛṣṇadās at the Bombay Veṅkaṭeśvara Steam Press' (U1 p. 182); (3) Tripathī's own 1965 volume was issued by Gangāviṣṇu Śrīkṛṣṇadāsa at Kalyāṇ — the OTHER brother's imprint; (4) Ullrey's bibliography carries a 2005 Khemarāja Śrīkṛṣṇadāsa printing of an Āścaryayogamālātantra ascribed to 'the perennial author Nāgārjuna'. One publishing family, four operative titles, a century and a third. The Lucknow parallel — Munshi Naval Kishore's press, founded 1858, the subcontinent's foremost house — is the other half of the picture and has a standing monograph in Stark (2007), NOT read this round.

procedures.typeAsFiled: channel-level: the mass reproduction of operative texts without critical apparatus
procedures.completenessBasis: the channel's effect on completeness is the finding: it FIXES uncritical witnesses as the standard text
procedures.evidence: Ullrey's Uḍḍīśatantra case is the demonstration. Three published recensions; no identified manuscript attestation for any of them; provenance left unspecified or elliptically described by publishers, editors and commentators; one commentator possibly working not from manuscripts at all but from earlier poor prints (U1 pp. 181, 186). The bazaar print is not a window onto a manuscript tradition — for most of this corpus it IS the tradition's surviving form, and the scholarly apparatus that would let anyone see past it does not exist.
procedures.harmNote: REQUIRED, and it is the sharpest harm point in the slice. Ṣaṭkarman material including māraṇa and vaśīkaraṇa circulates in cheap mass-market form with no gatekeeping and, in the modern Hindi commentaries, with the initiation requirement rhetorically retained while the text is sold to anyone. Recorded as a fact about the trade.

contested.flag: What the modern Hindi commentators are doing to the material.

positions.value: A documented RECODING, described at U1 pp. 187-189: the interpretation is pushed 'toward a modern, apologetic representation of the magic tantras'; it aligns with 'the dominant paradigm in contemporary emic tantra magic discourse, which is modern, psychological, and consistent with orthodox, translocal Hinduism'; 'Rituals whose results alter the physical world are re-coded as psychological'; 'Literal practice and interpretation of magic is rarely encouraged and is usually prohibited'; the commentator 'describes performing rituals only for socially positive results… and stresses mental performance', importing modern frames (bewildering as hypnotism, dissension as political ideology). Ullrey's summary formula: 'The anesthetizing of tantra continues in the present, but aestheticization is replaced by mental act akin to Protestant prayer.' And the reader's actual use of the Sanskrit: 'modern pandits cheerfully extract the mantras from the rituals; after all, tantras are considered mere strong-boxes to preserve and transmit the mantras.'

he refuses to treat this as decline or as mere colonial contamination — 'South Asians interpret tantra from the inside; their interpretations are valid developments in the tantra tradition throughout South Asia' (p. 189 n.109), and he notes that literal practice 'continue[s] to be practiced outside urbane environments… in villages, remote areas, and by/for urban non-elites' (p. 189).

contested.note: Both positions are the same scholar's, held together deliberately. The slice does not adjudicate, and in particular does not endorse either 'the moderns have watered it down' or 'the moderns have cleaned it up'. The named commentators are recent or living.

That sequence is the evidentiary anchor for every 'licence to depart' claim in this slice, and it comes from a JAIN text, not from the Bhūtaḍāmaratantra.

procedures.typeAsFiled: five-fold ritual sequence terminating in dismissal (visarjana)
procedures.completenessBasis: the sequence is stated as an explicit rule in a single verse, and that verse was read in a scholar's translation
procedures.evidence: U1 p. 576 n.51 gives the verse's content as a five-member enumeration and locates it at 3.24; Ullrey's own Appendix Two translates the BPK in full. The Sanskrit of the enumeration and the dismissal formula are both printed in Ullrey and are NOT reproduced here.

Named as an Uḍḍ-corpus ancillary at U1 p. 182 n.93 and counted by Goudriaan among the four Uḍḍīśa parents (U1 p. 194 n.118). Contents not examined.

The corpus's colophons make this claim, and make the reverse claim, and make it of several other texts. U1 p. 194: 'Almost every Uḍḍ-corpus text claims the Vīrabhadratantra as a source, yet several chapters of an Uḍḍīśatantra will claim the Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra as a source and vice versa'; published colophons have been editorially normalised. A source-claim here is a genre gesture. NOT a documented dependency.

Zadoo ch.1 colophon states the Uḍḍāmareśvara mahātantra is derived from the Vīrabhadreśvaratantra (U1 p. 194 n.118). Same objection as above: the corpus's colophons contradict one another and the printed ones are normalised.

One Uḍḍīśatantra manuscript often closer resembles various Uḍḍāmaratantras, and a single Uḍḍāmeśvaratantra often contains identical content from numerous Uḍḍīśatantras.' This is a symmetric content-sharing edge, NOT a directed dependency, and is asserted only as such.

edges.basis: DOCUMENTED DEPENDENCY — chapter-level collation plus manuscript-error inheritance
edges.evidence: THE STRONGEST TRANSMISSION EDGE IN THE SLICE, and the only one resting on inherited errors. (1) Bhattacharyya (1933) tabulated the two recensions' chapters side by side and showed the Śaiva text incorporating and augmenting the Buddhist one (U1 pp. 553-554). (3) Corroborating direction-markers: the Śaiva version encodes mantras where the Buddhist writes them plainly, and encoding indicates posteriority; the Śaiva recasts prose as verse; the Śaiva retains Buddhist deity names inside its mantras and Buddhist worship-sites in its place-names while deleting Buddhist doctrine; and the Śaiva retains subjugation and murder rites against high Hindu gods, 'unheard of in an originally Hindu tantra'.

edges.basis: STRUCTURAL, EVIDENCED, AND EXPLICITLY NOT GENEALOGICAL — this is the slice's headline comparison and it is deliberately fenced
edges.evidence: Four structural correspondences, each independently sourced, none implying contact. (1) A NAMED, RANKED HIERARCHY: the Buddhist recension organises its material by spirit pantheon in 'a loose, over-arching maṇḍala of being, ranging from dryads (yakṣiṇī) to demons (bhūtinī) to snakes (nāginī)', with eight named Demon Princesses (aṣṭamahābhūtarajñā) heading their own cycle of eight indexed rites (U1 pp. 552, 575). Compare the Ars Goetia's ranked, individually named and individually rited spirit list. (2) A COMPELLING PROCEDURE WITH A COERCIVE SANCTION: the rite compels appearance, and the text states a destructive consequence for non-appearance and for non-service (U1 pp. 575-576). Compare the Goetic constraint and the curses of the Solomonic conjuration sequence. (3) A SERVITOR OUTCOME: the declared result is enslavement (kiṃkarī), and the tantra carries a distinct kiṃkara-sādhana making rival-tradition gods into slaves (U1 p. 600). Compare the Goetic office-and-service structure. (4) A DISMISSAL TERMINUS — WITH THE SLICE'S OWN CAVEAT: the five-fold sequence ending in visarjana is documented for this ritual grammar and Ullrey reads the tantra's gesture-set as echoing it, but the anchoring verse is Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa 3.24, a Jain text, and no source read this round locates a dismissal rubric inside the Bhūtaḍāmaratantra (U1 p. 576 + n.51). Correspondence (4) is therefore the weak leg and is flagged as such rather than quietly carried.
edges.assertionScope: The edge asserts a STRUCTURAL PARALLEL as an observation of this slice. It asserts no contact, no shared source, no influence and no common origin in either direction.

edges.basis: DECLINED — no documented dependency in either direction
edges.evidence: The only printed linkage located between the Indian operative corpus and the Goetia is Ullrey's own footnote (U1 pp. 190-191 n.112), and it is a SEMANTIC aside, not a textual claim: sorcerers and powerful female beings are characteristically NOISY, ḍākinī may derive from √ḍam 'to sound' rather than *ḍī 'to fly', and the Greek goēs is a howler — from which he glances at 'the modern occult references to the power-daemons of Goetia'. TWO INDEPENDENT REASONS THE EDGE FAILS. First, the etymology it rests on is a minority one: White, whom Ullrey cites, presents ḍam as 'suggested' against 'the more widely accepted' *ḍi. Second, and decisively, a shared semantic field of noisiness is not a textual dependency at all. Ullrey himself supplies the governing methodological rule at p. 192: 'Etymology similarities in titles does not establish connection; texts must reproduce cognate verses and/or content to establish connection' — and at p. 193 n.117, following J.Z. Smith and Hassan, that comparison yields affinity, not influence, and that 'subjective experience is projected as an objective connection through some theory of influence, diffusion, borrowing, or the like.' No cognate verses, no shared content, no contact. DECLINED, and it should stay declined.

For most of this corpus the cheap print is not a witness to the tradition — it is the tradition's surviving form.

structuralFindings.finding: SYSTEMATIC vs ENCYCLOPEDIC is the corpus's real formal division, and it is a completeness axis.
structuralFindings.detail: Encyclopedic tantras catalogue discrete short rites grouped by RESULT — 'They are cookbooks, grimoire catalogs' (U1 p. 158). Systematic tantras correlate VARIABLES to results and are second-order: 'They are the culinary arts, magic principles, theory, lore, magic śāstra' (p. 157). Three encyclopedic composition strategies: three-part discrete verses carrying ritual action + mantra + result; long discrete verses; and simple discrete verses lacking one of the three parts. Three systematic strategies: the 'systematic variable' (a variable-set mapped to a result-set), the 'rolling variable' (one rite followed by verses each altering one element to shift the result), and 'lore' (ranking, symptomatology, substitution, and what to do when nothing happens). Ullrey's own image for his choice of subject: 'I study cooks, not chefs; sorcerers, not pandits' (p. 159).
structuralFindings.whyItMatters: A completeness grade means different things on the two sides. An encyclopedic rite is complete when it carries all three parts; a systematic passage is complete when its variable-set closes. Grading them on one scale is the error this slice's `completenessBasis` field exists to prevent.

structuralFindings.finding: THE INDEX-VERSE MISMATCH: a magic tantra's own table of contents routinely does not describe it.
structuralFindings.detail: All three published Uḍḍīśatantras print a six-item index verse; their bodies deliver eight, seven and seven results respectively, in three different orders, and in two of the three the first headed topic is MURDER. Zadoo's Uḍḍāmareśvara prints four mutually inconsistent organising passages before its body begins. Ullrey: 'Index verses differing from actual contents of the text is common, if not universal, in magic tantras' (p. 183 n.95); 'Index lists, in fact, rarely present a text's contents accurately' (p. 148).
structuralFindings.whyItMatters: It forbids a whole class of cheap research move. No completeness or contents claim about a text in this corpus may be derived from its index verse, its title, or a catalogue entry copying either. Every grade in this slice that rests on a heading rather than a reading is marked accordingly.

structuralFindings.finding: DELIBERATE WITHHOLDING IS BUILT INTO THE TEXTS, and it takes at least three distinct forms.
structuralFindings.detail: (1) MANTRA ENCODING (mantroddhāra/mantrakośa): the Śaiva Bhūtaḍāmara substitutes coded epithets for the syllables its Buddhist source writes out plainly — the text is whole and unusable without a key held by an initiator. (2) THE GURU CLAUSE: the Uḍḍīśatantra's opening states in its own voice that wisdom written in a book confers nothing, and that without a guru there is no authority in scripture — a printed book denying the sufficiency of printed books. (3) EDITORIAL SUPPRESSION IN PRINT: Goudriaan suspected 'deliberate omission by the editors' in the 1915 Indrajālavidyāsaṃgraha; Ullrey partly demurs, attributing the gaps instead to ordinary transmission and to 'awkward seams where material is inserted or tacked on artlessly'. Both explanations are recorded.
structuralFindings.whyItMatters: Incompleteness in this corpus is frequently a FEATURE and must be graded as such rather than as damage — and the repo now has an Indian analogue to the cipher-and-notarikon withholding of the Western grimoire tradition.

structuralFindings.finding: THE PRINT-TRADE IS THE TRANSMISSION, and it is nameable.
structuralFindings.detail: One Marwari publishing family — Gangavishnu and Khemraj Bajaj of Churu, Mumbai from 1868, Moti Bazar 1871, Khetwadi 1880, separating 1893 — printed the 1899 Kāmaratnam with its 27 plates of yantras, the Venkateshvar Steam Press Uḍḍīśatantra that Tripathī reproduces, Tripathī's own 1965 volume under the other brother's Kalyāṇ imprint, and a 2005 Nāgārjuna-branded tantra. Meanwhile no published Uḍḍīśatantra recension has an identified manuscript attestation, and one may have been assembled from earlier prints rather than from manuscripts at all.
structuralFindings.whyItMatters: This is the Indian counterpart of the cheap chapbook grimoire, and it is better documented at the imprint level than at the textual level — the reverse of the Western case, where the texts are edited and the print history is often the murky part.

structuralFindings.finding: THE GOETIA PARALLEL IS STRUCTURAL AND HAS EXACTLY ONE WEAK LEG.
structuralFindings.detail: Named ranked hierarchy: EVIDENCED. Compelling procedure with coercive sanction: EVIDENCED. Servitor/office outcome: EVIDENCED. Dismissal terminus: ATTESTED FOR THE RITUAL GRAMMAR, from a Jain text, and NOT located inside the Bhūtaḍāmaratantra by any source read. Transmission in either direction: NO EVIDENCE, and the only printed linkage is a semantic aside resting on a minority etymology of ḍākinī.
structuralFindings.whyItMatters: The comparison is worth making and worth fencing. Ullrey supplies the fence himself: 'Etymology similarities in titles does not establish connection; texts must reproduce cognate verses and/or content to establish connection' (p. 192), and — after J.Z. Smith and Hassan — comparison yields affinity, not influence (p. 193 n.117).

structuralFindings.finding: 'KERALA MANTRAVĀDA' IS NOT WHERE THE BRIEF EXPECTED IT.
structuralFindings.detail: The two famous Kerala manuals named in the brief — Tantrasamuccaya and Prayogamañjarī — are TEMPLE-RITUAL paddhatis: construction, installation, liṅga worship, renovation, festival, expiation. No source read this round places ṣaṭkarman or abhicāra material in either. The Kerala operative material sits in the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati's Mantrapāda and, above all, in Nārāyaṇa's Tantrasārasaṃgraha (Viṣanārāyaṇīya): 32 chapters, ten of them toxicology, the rest spirit-affliction, madness, COUNTER-sorcery, and desire-directed acts.
structuralFindings.whyItMatters: Two consequences. First, the Kerala operative corpus has a DEFENCE-WEIGHTED shape — poison, possession, madness, counter-sorcery — quite unlike the Uḍḍ-corpus, where murder heads the body-text; that difference must not be flattened into one 'Indian grimoire' profile. Second, in this corpus the word 'tantra' in a title predicts nothing about contents.

structuralFindings.finding: THE CORPUS PROVIDES ITS OWN BIBLIOGRAPHY — and it cannot be trusted as one.
structuralFindings.detail: The Dattātreyatantra opens by naming where operative material lives (Āgamas, Purāṇas, Vedas, Ḍāmara scriptures) and then names titles: Uḍḍīśa, Merutantra, Kālacaṇḍeśvara, Rādhātantra, Tāratantra, Amṛteśvara. Uḍḍ-corpus colophons name each other and the Vīrabhadratantra in every direction at once, and printed colophons have been editorially normalised.
structuralFindings.whyItMatters: These self-citations are genuine evidence of a self-aware genre and of an emic map — including two bridges into S10's philosophical corpus — but they are NOT citations in the bibliographic sense, and no derivation edge in this slice rests on one.

structuralFindings.finding: SHARED ERROR, NOT SHARED CONTENT, IS WHAT MAKES A DEPENDENCY HERE.
structuralFindings.detail: The slice's one strong transmission edge — Buddhist Bhūtaḍāmara → Śaiva Bhūtaḍāmara — rests on Śaiva manuscripts reproducing errors found in LATE Buddhist versions that postdate the Tibetan translation, corroborated by mantra-encoding, prose-to-verse reformatting, retained Buddhist deity-names inside mantras, retained Buddhist place-names, deleted Buddhist doctrine, and retained rites against high Hindu gods. Every other candidate transmission edge in the slice rests on shared goddess-lists, and Ullrey warns that such lists 'are not standard, contain both real and fanciful names, and often represent borrowed materials with no semantic value'.
structuralFindings.whyItMatters: It gives the slice a bright line, and the line is why the repo's existing 'Bhūtaḍāmara feeds the Uḍḍīśa material' record is downgraded here to a symmetric content-sharing edge.

notes: NOTHING IN THIS FILE IS AN INSTRUCTION. The corpus catalogued here is dense with rites aimed at named living persons, including lethal ones. No mantra syllable, seed-syllable string, ingredient, quantity, repetition-count, timing, site-preparation, yantra template or target-naming formula appears anywhere in this file, and the sources it draws on print all of them.

EFFICACY IS NEVER ASSERTED. The tradition claims; the text says. Ullrey, this slice's principal source, states at p. 633: 'Do the magic operations confer the results declared? Well no, they don't. Magic doesn't work.'

The Uḍḍīśatantra's opening declares in its own voice that no wisdom written in a book confers perfection and that without a guru there is no authority in scripture (Tripathī 1.7). It is worth recording that the corpus's own frame denies the sufficiency of the printed page — in a text that survives almost entirely as printed pages.
